job.style: a passage that starts from a common wrong idea and corrects it

passage: Many people believe that sound waves travel through the air like ripples moving up and down on a string, but this is incorrect. Sound is actually a longitudinal wave where particles vibrate back and forth in the same direction the wave travels. This movement creates regions of high pressure called compressions and regions of low pressure called rarefactions, which still contain plenty of air particles. Because sound requires a physical medium to vibrate, it cannot travel through the vacuum of outer space, no matter how massive an explosion occurs. Furthermore, the speed of sound is not a universal constant like light; it changes depending on the material it moves through. Sound travels significantly faster in solids than in air because the particles in a solid are packed closely together, allowing vibrations to pass more efficiently. Finally, remember that the speed of a sound wave remains constant for a given medium, even if you increase the frequency or pitch of the sound. Loudness is determined by the amplitude of the vibration, not by how fast the source vibrates or how high the pitch is. Understanding these mechanics helps us see why sound behaves differently than light or simple surface waves.

items.evidence: This movement creates regions of high pressure called compressions and regions of low pressure called rarefactions, which still contain plenty of air particles.
items.q: A tiny probe sits inside a rarefaction of a sound wave in air. What will it find?
options: Air particles at lower pressure than usual
No air particles, only empty space
Air particles at the highest pressure
Air particles moving only up and down
items.explain: Rarefactions are low-pressure regions, but they still contain plenty of air particles.

wrong.why: thinks a rarefaction has no particles at all
thinks sound moves up and down like a string wave

items.evidence: Because sound requires a physical medium to vibrate, it cannot travel through the vacuum of outer space, no matter how massive an explosion occurs.
items.q: Why can't the sound of an explosion in outer space reach a nearby astronaut?
options: There is no medium there to vibrate
The explosion is not big enough there
Sound moves too fast there, like light
Its frequency is too high to travel there
items.explain: Sound needs a medium to vibrate. Space is a vacuum, so even a huge explosion is silent.

wrong.why: thinks a big enough explosion can be heard in space
wrongly links frequency to how sound travels

items.evidence: Sound travels significantly faster in solids than in air because the particles in a solid are packed closely together, allowing vibrations to pass more efficiently.
items.q: Meena presses her ear to an iron rail as a friend taps the far end. How does that sound travel?
options: Faster than in air, as particles are close
Slower than in air, as iron is too dense
Same as in air, since sound speed is fixed
Faster than in air, due to its higher pitch
items.explain: Particles in a solid are packed closely, so vibrations pass faster than in air.

wrong.why: thinks solids are too dense for sound
thinks the speed of sound never changes
thinks higher pitch makes sound faster

items.evidence: Loudness is determined by the amplitude of the vibration, not by how fast the source vibrates or how high the pitch is.
items.q: Asha makes her drum sound louder without changing its pitch. What has she changed?
options: How far the drum skin moves when vibrating
How fast the drum skin vibrates each second
How fast the sound wave moves through air
How high the note of the drum sounds
items.explain: Loudness depends on amplitude, meaning how far the skin moves, not on how fast it vibrates.

wrong.why: thinks loudness depends on how fast the source vibrates
